summary: The 1949 Robot Light, an automated Coast Guard beacon at the end of the Long Beach breakwater, California; never manned, closed to visitors, seen from boats.

light.characteristic: one-second flash every four seconds (1951 description; the station record gives Fl W 5s)
light.fog_signal: diaphragm horn, three-second blast every 20 seconds (1951); blasts every 30 seconds (2019)

structures.note: Rectangular white concrete house, barely 20 ft square at the base, mounted on piles; light raised 50 ft above mean low water (1951). Three-story monolithic concrete structure (LHF).
The earlier skeletal tower was moved across the harbor entrance to mark the western side of the channel, once the new light was active (LHF). Date and build history not found in the sources read.

access.note: Coast Guard property. Grounds and tower closed to the public. Best viewed from a boat, or from shore at Ocean Boulevard and Cherry Avenue.

events.note: Long Beach Breakwater Light: electric light fed by a cable of about 10,000 feet laid by the city of Long Beach. Heavy seas broke the cable; a temporary acetylene light was placed on the end of the breakwater.
Southern California earthquake from 10 March 1933. Keepers' reports say no damage to the structures at stations that reported. The breakwater light is not named.
Established at its present site in 1949 (typed sheet). Completed 1949 (LHF).
Robot light, operated by remote control from the Los Angeles Harbor light (1951; LHF).
Modernized in 1972 and 1973; new monitoring equipment installed (typed sheet).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1951 article gives a three-second blast every 20 seconds; the Coast Guard's officer in 2019 says the signal blasts every 30 seconds. Both can be right at different dates; the 30-second interval is the current one reported.

LighthouseFriends gives roughly $200,000 for the completed station; the 1951 article calls it a new $200,000 station. The sources agree. An earlier draft's '$290,000' was a misreading of the 1951 article (checked on the page image 2026-10-28) and is removed.

notes_for_editor: Read before publishing. Fact-checked 2026-10-28. (1) SCANS: sources 2 and 3 are scanned images with no text layer (Robot Light.pdf). The quote checker cannot read them, so every quotation from them was checked by hand against a 300-dpi render of the page image on 2026-10-28. One was wrong: the 1951 article says 'new $200,000 station', not '$290,000'. That error, and the cost 'disagreement' built on it, are removed: LighthouseFriends gives roughly $200,000 and the article agrees. (2) The 1951 article (Ships & Sailing, July 1951) is treated as copyrighted: the story paraphrases it; the one quotation kept is 'barely 20 feet' in paraphrase form only. (3) Source 3 (typed station sheet) is unsigned and undated; the story says so. (4) GENERATOR INTERVAL: LighthouseFriends says twelve-hour intervals; the 1951 article says every four hours. Both are stated; not resolved. (5) FOG SIGNAL: LighthouseFriends describes 17-inch Tyfon foghorns run by gasoline compressors; the 1951 article describes a diaphragm horn with a three-second blast every 20 seconds; the 2019 Beachcomber says it blasts every 30 seconds. The story states the first two as different accounts. (6) RANGE: the 1951 article says visible 13 miles and does not say nautical; the station record gives 14 nm. (7) CHARACTERISTIC: the station record says Fl W 5s (ENC); the 1951 article says one flash of one second every four seconds. The current Light List entry was not read; do not change the record on the 1951 figures. (8) EARLIER LIGHT: the 1931 Bulletin's breakwater light is not confirmed as LighthouseFriends' earlier skeletal tower; no date is given for that tower. (9) USLHS PLACE RECORD: its coordinates are malformed (33 deg 72.32 min); do not use them. It says Open to Public: No. (10) PEOPLE: Laird, Hendrix and Shey are named only as the 1951 article names them, in public roles. The 2019 Coast Guard petty officer is not named. (11) The Beachcomber (2019) and LighthouseFriends are copyrighted: the story paraphrases them, keeping one short quotation ('blasts every 30 seconds'). (12) PHOTOS: the record has a Wikimedia Commons photo (USCG 1949); its licence was not checked, so it is not added. (13) The 1951 article describes the light as operated by remote control from a mainland station five miles away; it names no keeper there. SHAPE: six chapters for about 930 words is above the moderate band (2-4 chapters); left for the writer to decide whether to merge. Quotations from the 1951 article, LighthouseFriends and the Beachcomber were reduced to paraphrase, as the copyright rule for these sources requires.
